Do Now

U.S. Peace Commissioners meeting with Native leaders during the 1868 Fort Laramie Treaty negotiations. Photograph by Alexander Gardner.

During the mid-1800s, the U.S. government signed dozens of treaties with Native nations — legally binding agreements, ratified by the Senate, carrying the same legal weight as a treaty with any foreign country. In practice, they were broken constantly: settlers moved onto treaty land before the ink dried, Congress passed laws that quietly overrode treaty terms, and when something valuable turned up on land the U.S. had already promised away — gold, fertile farmland, a railroad route — the government usually found a way to take it back. In 1871, Congress stopped making treaties with tribes altogether, declaring that Native nations would no longer be negotiated with as sovereign powers — only governed by statute, like a territory.

In 1868, the U.S. government signed the Fort Laramie Treaty with the Lakota, promising them the Black Hills "as long as the grass shall grow and the water flow." In 1874, gold was discovered there.

Predict: what do you think happens next? Write 2–3 sentences — no research needed, just your best guess.

After Four Corners

A treaty is a formal, legally binding agreement between two governments — not a handshake or an understanding, but a signed document both sides are supposed to honor no matter what happens later.

Your class discussed this scenario: "Two nations sign a 50-year treaty giving one people fishing rights to a shared lake. Ten years in, the other nation discovers oil beneath that lake — worth far more than the fish ever were. Would it be okay for one nation to opt out of the treaty since something new and important was discovered?"

This kind of thing happens outside of treaties too. A company signs a 30-year lease on a farmer's land, then a huge natural gas deposit is discovered underneath it. Two business partners agree to split profits evenly, then one of them invents something that makes the company worth ten times more than before. A landlord signs a 10-year lease, then the neighborhood becomes so popular that the same building could rent for triple the price. In each case: something nobody knew about at the time changes how good or bad the original deal looks.

Where do you personally land?

Document 1: Two Accounts of One Battle — Little Bighorn, June 25, 1876

This is the first time this unit has looked closely at armed Native resistance. By 1876, the U.S. Army had spent years pushing the Lakota, Cheyenne, and other Plains nations off land guaranteed to them by treaty — accelerated by the discovery of gold in the Black Hills two years earlier (the very treaty violation you just predicted in the Do Now). Lieutenant Colonel George Armstrong Custer led the U.S. 7th Cavalry against a large encampment of Lakota and Cheyenne gathered along the Little Bighorn River in Montana Territory. Custer and roughly 268 of his men were killed — the worst defeat the U.S. Army suffered in the Plains wars. What follows are two accounts of that day. Read both fully before forming an opinion about either.

Lt. Col. George Armstrong Custer, U.S. 7th Cavalry.
Sitting Bull, Hunkpapa Lakota spiritual leader — present at the camp but not a battle commander. He had had a vision of soldiers falling days earlier at the Sun Dance. Photo by D. F. Barry, c. 1883.
Source A
NEW YORK HERALD, front page, September 2, 1876:

"GENERAL CUSTER KILLED... THE ENTIRE DETACHMENT UNDER HIS COMMAND SLAUGHTERED..."

Coverage across the country followed the same pattern in the weeks after: Custer was mourned nationwide as a fallen hero cut down by treachery, and the Lakota and Cheyenne fighters were repeatedly described as a savage horde acting without provocation — regardless of the actual events at the encampment.
Source B
Two Moon (Northern Cheyenne war chief), recalling the battle in an 1898 interview with writer Hamlin Garland, published in McClure's Magazine — 22 years after the battle:

Two Moon described his people camped peacefully along the river, preparing for a feast, when Custer's cavalry attacked without warning. He recalled women and children running for the hills before the men could even saddle their horses, and remembered the fighting itself as chaotic and desperate — his people defending their camp, not attacking anyone. By the time it ended, he said, the ground was littered with the dead and dying.
Little Bighorn Battlefield today — the white markers show where U.S. soldiers fell.
Two Moon, Northern Cheyenne war chief and source of the account above.

What happened next

Little Bighorn was a stunning Lakota and Cheyenne victory — and it backfired almost immediately. Rather than making the U.S. Army back off, news of Custer's defeat triggered public outrage across the country and a demand for revenge. Congress approved more troops and money, and within a year the Army had hunted down or forced the surrender of most of the war leaders who had fought at the river that day.

Why might winning this battle so completely have made things worse, not better, for the Lakota and Cheyenne in the long run?

Close Read: "I Will Fight No More Forever" — October 5, 1877

After Little Bighorn, the U.S. Army pursued Native resistance across the Plains. One of the final holdouts was Chief Joseph of the Nez Perce, who led roughly 750 of his people on a 1,170-mile flight toward Canada, hoping to escape onto Sitting Bull's land — but was stopped just 40 miles short of the border.

Chief Joseph (Heinmot Tooyalakekt), photographed in 1903 by Edward S. Curtis. National Portrait Gallery, Smithsonian Institution. Public domain.
Map of the Nez Perce Outbreak and War, June-October 1877, showing the flight route from Wallowa Valley through White Bird Canyon, Big Hole, Canyon Creek, and the final battle at Bear Paw.
"My people, some of them, have run away to the hills, and have no blankets, no food; no one knows where they are — perhaps freezing to death. I want to have time to look for my children, and see how many of them I can find. Maybe I shall find them among the dead. Hear me, my chiefs! I am tired; my heart is sick and sad. From where the sun now stands, I will fight no more forever."

Close read

Whose words are these, really?

Chief Joseph spoke only Nez Perce. His words were passed through at least one interpreter, then written down by Lieutenant Charles Erskine Scott Wood — a U.S. Army officer who later became a published poet. Historians still argue over how much of this speech is Joseph's own meaning and how much is Wood's literary polish. No version in Joseph's own hand exists.

Given what you just read, should this still count as a reliable historical source? Why or why not?

What Happened to the Land

After resistance ended, the government's main tool changed — from war to a different kind of pressure. In 1887, Congress passed the Dawes Act. It broke up reservation land — previously held in common by the tribe — into individual allotments, up to 160 acres per family. Any land left over after allotting was declared "surplus" and opened to white settlers. The government held each allotment in federal trust for 25 years, and any Native person who accepted one was automatically declared a U.S. citizen. This is the allotment and reservation vocabulary from this morning, now attached to an actual law with real consequences.

Indian Land Cessions in the United States, by Sam B. Hilliard. The bottom-right panel (1880–1972) shows land loss continuing well past the Dawes Act era. Even without reading every label, the shrinking colored areas over time tell the story.
Green = individual Native-held allotments  |  Pink = "surplus" land sold to settlers, checkerboarding the reservation
Political cartoon by Marty Two Bulls, 2012.

This cartoon, drawn in 2012, shows the Dawes Act as a monster with the words "CHOMP CHOMP CHOMP" eating "INDIAN LANDS." What point is the cartoonist making? Do you think this is a fair way to depict this history, or does it oversimplify it? Why?

Practical: Why might breaking communal land into individual plots make it easier for the government to eventually open reservation land to outside settlers?

Document 2: "Kill the Indian, Save the Man" — Carlisle, 1879–1918

By the late 1870s, the U.S. government had a new problem: thousands of Native people who had survived the wars, but whose land and old way of life were mostly gone. Some officials wanted them removed or left to die out. Others believed the answer was assimilation — teaching Native children to speak English, dress, worship, and live like white Americans, so they could "join" mainstream society instead of being destroyed by it. Starting in 1879, the government built a system of off-reservation boarding schools to do exactly that. Over 350 of these schools eventually operated across the country.

Richard Henry Pratt, founder of the Carlisle Indian Industrial School.

Richard Henry Pratt, an Army officer, ran the first of these schools, in Carlisle, Pennsylvania. Pratt had previously overseen Native prisoners of war and became convinced that total immersion in white culture — not confinement, and not extermination — was the only way to help Native people survive in a country that was not going to stop expanding. He recruited students directly from reservations, sometimes as a condition attached to broader negotiations with tribal leaders. Carlisle became the model for the entire system.

Native American children at a government boarding school. Hover the numbered dots.

Carlisle was founded in 1879 by Richard Henry Pratt, a former Army officer. In 1892, responding to a general who had said "the only good Indian is a dead one," Pratt offered what he believed was the humane alternative:

"In a sense, I agree with the sentiment, but only in this: that all the Indian there is in the race should be dead. Kill the Indian in him, and save the man."

Before and after: what changed

CategoryBefore CarlisleAt Carlisle
LanguageNative language spoken freelyEnglish only, everywhere on campus
HairOften worn long — spiritual/personal meaningCut short on arrival
ClothingTribal dressMilitary-style uniforms
NameGiven/tribal nameAssigned an English name, often at random
Contact with familyDaily life with parents and communityLetters home often withheld or delayed by agents; visits rare

In a student's own words

"The civilizing process at Carlisle began with clothes. Whites believed the Indian children could not be civilized while wearing moccasins and blankets. Their hair was cut because in some mysterious way long hair stood in the path of our development. They were issued the clothes of white men. High collar stiff-bosomed shirts and suspenders fully three inches in width were uncomfortable. White leather boots caused actual suffering." He remembered the red flannel underwear the school issued as "the worst thing about life at Carlisle."

— Luther Standing Bear (Sicangu-Oglala Lakota), one of the first students, arrived 1879
Luther Standing Bear with his father, George Standing Bear, at Carlisle, c. 1890.

Standing Bear says his hair was cut "because in some mysterious way long hair stood in the path of our development." What is he suggesting about the school's real reasoning, versus its stated reasoning?

Why might a memoir written years later include small physical details -- stiff collars, red flannel underwear -- rather than just saying the experience was hard?

One student: Tom Torlino

Tom Torlino, a young Navajo man, arrived at Carlisle on October 21, 1882. The school's photographer took his portrait that day — and again three and a half years later, just before Torlino left in August 1886.

Tom Torlino, Navajo. Photographs by John N. Choate, Carlisle Indian Industrial School, 1882 and 1885. Carlisle Indian School Digital Resource Center / National Archives. Public domain.

What Should the Government Have Done?

By the 1880s, the U.S. government faced a decision it had been avoiding for decades: what should its actual policy toward Native nations be? Below are four real positions that were seriously debated at the time. Read all four, then rank them 1st (most justified) through 4th (least justified) given what people knew then — not what we know now. Click a rank number on each card; the cards will reorder as you go.

1. Forced Assimilation (Pratt's model — Carlisle)

Pros
  • Framed by supporters as the humane alternative to extermination
  • Aimed to give Native people the language/skills to survive in the new economy
  • Some students left with real trades and literacy
Cons
  • Destroyed languages, family bonds, and cultural identity by design
  • Treated Native culture itself as the problem to be solved
  • Often carried out by force, without real consent

2. Removal / Extermination (the hardline military position)

Pros (as its supporters argued)
  • Claimed to be the fastest way to end the wars
  • Freed up land for settlement immediately
Cons
  • Explicitly genocidal in intent for some proponents
  • Violated treaties already signed and ratified
  • Caused massive civilian death — Sand Creek, Wounded Knee

3. Honor Existing Treaties / Tribal Self-Governance

Pros
  • Kept the government's word
  • Preserved Native sovereignty and culture
  • What most Native leaders were actually asking for
Cons
  • Required saying no to settlers, miners, and railroads — politically very difficult
  • Some treaty boundaries had never been clearly surveyed or agreed on by all parties

4. Allotment + Automatic Citizenship (the actual compromise — Dawes Act)

Pros
  • Framed as a middle path between removal and reservation confinement
  • Gave individual land ownership and full citizenship
Cons
  • Massively accelerated communal land loss
  • "Surplus" land went to settlers anyway
  • Imposed citizenship without real consent, as a condition of losing land

Closing: The Wars End

What historians usually call the "Indian Wars" was not one war but a scattered, three-decade string of raids, broken treaties, and massacres across the Plains, from the early 1860s to 1890. There was no single declaration of war and no single peace treaty ending it — it simply wound down as Native nations ran out of land, food, and options, and as the government's policy shifted toward the assimilation you just read about — the same word from this morning's vocab check-in, now with a whole document's worth of evidence behind it. The two events below bookend that period: one near its start, one at its end, and both in the same pattern.

Context: Sand Creek, Colorado — November 29, 1864

Sand Creek Massacre, painting by Robert Lindneux, 1936. History Colorado.
The Sand Creek Massacre site, southeastern Colorado.
Colonel John Chivington, Third Colorado Cavalry.
A delegation of Arapaho and Cheyenne leaders met with the U.S. military on Sept. 28, 1864, at Camp Weld, Colo., to seek peace on the plains east of Denver, almost two months before the Sand Creek Massacre. Denver Public Library, Western History Collection.

This happened here, over a decade before Little Bighorn. Colonel John Chivington led the Third Colorado Cavalry in a surprise attack on a peaceful camp of Cheyenne and Arapaho led by Chief Black Kettle — who was flying both the American flag and a white flag of truce, exactly as U.S. officials had instructed. An estimated 150–230 people were killed, most of them women, children, and the elderly. Just two months earlier, Arapaho and Cheyenne leaders had traveled to Camp Weld, near Denver, specifically to negotiate peace.

Context: it wasn't only one-sided

Native nations did kill settlers too, and it matters to understand why. The largest example is the Dakota War of 1862 in Minnesota — not on the Plains, but nearby in both time and cause. For years, the U.S. had delayed and shorted the Dakota's treaty annuity payments (money and goods owed under treaty), while traders inflated debts and settlers kept moving onto Dakota land. Facing starvation, Dakota leader Little Crow led attacks on settlements that killed an estimated 400-800 settlers over six weeks. The U.S. response was to hang 38 Dakota men in one day - the largest mass execution in American history - and expel the entire Dakota nation from Minnesota. The motivation was real desperation over broken promises; the method still killed civilians who had not made those promises. Both things can be true at once.

Wounded Knee, South Dakota — December 29, 1890

"Burial of the Dead at the Battle of Wounded Knee, S.D." Photo by North Western Photo Co., Chadron, Nebraska, c. 1891. Public domain.

At Wounded Knee Creek, U.S. troops killed an estimated 150–300 Lakota men, women, and children — the last major armed confrontation between the U.S. Army and Native nations on the Plains. It happened 26 years after Sand Creek, and just three years after Carlisle's model had already spread to dozens of schools.

Ken Burns documentary, background on Sitting Bull and Wounded Knee, ~6 min.

Sand Creek (1864) and Wounded Knee (1890) happened 26 years apart, in different states, under different commanders. What's the same about both? What's different?

One Hard Question

AI-generated illustration, made for this lesson — not a historical photograph or painting. It depicts two real, documented battles: the Grapevine Creek Battle (Crow vs. Blackfeet, near present-day Fort C.F. Smith, Montana, c. 1850) and the Fetterman Fight (Lakota, Cheyenne, and Arapaho forces vs. the U.S. Army near Fort Phil Kearny, Wyoming, December 21, 1866).

Native nations fought each other long before Europeans arrived. Before you answer the question below, here is what that intertribal conflict actually looked like, side by side with U.S.-Native warfare:

Intertribal warfare (common patterns)U.S. Army / federal government vs. Native nations
Scale Often small raiding parties, but sometimes large battles and attacks on villages Could mobilize sustained military campaigns drawing on the resources of the U.S. government
Typical goal Horses, captives, prestige, revenge, control of hunting territory/resources, or weakening rivals Defeat Native resistance and enforce U.S. control over territory; often force Native peoples onto reservations
What happened to the loser Outcomes varied: casualties, captives, lost resources, and sometimes displacement or loss of territory; defeated groups often remained politically and culturally independent Defeat could lead to permanent territorial loss, confinement to reservations, and eventually federal assimilation policies targeting tribal landholding, language, education, and culture
Broken promise? Varied — alliances and agreements existed, but not usually treaties backed by the legal authority of a nation-state The U.S. sometimes violated or unilaterally altered ratified treaties and agreements with Native nations

This is not to say intertribal conflict was gentle — people died, and some conflicts (like long-running revenge cycles) could be brutal and sustained. The comparison above is about scale, goal, and the presence of a broken legal promise — not about which side's warriors fought more bravely or more violently.

Is there a fundamental difference between Native nations fighting each other and the U.S. Army fighting Native nations — or is this just how wars between rival powers work? Defend your answer.
